column2: I'm sending this picture to a million phones. Each one randomly loses about one packet in a hundred.
Yet almost every phone that catches just two packets more than it needs rebuilds the picture exactly. The secret is an arithmetic where three times seven is nine.
A file travels as thousands of packets, each carrying one small piece of it. Our picture is cut into ten thousand pieces. Lose some, and the usual fix is to ask again.
With a million phones, each packet goes missing for about ten thousand of them, and the requests swamp the sender. A TV antenna can't ask at all.
So send the file on a loop. Miss a piece, and you wait a whole loop for it. Most phones need two or three loops. The unluckiest of a million need five or six.
Sending random pieces is worse. It's a sticker album. How many random pieces until you've seen all ten thousand?
On average, about ninety-eight thousand. The last few take forever, because you keep getting doubles.
First, how computers write numbers. Each spot holds a bit, a zero or a one, and each spot is worth double the one to its right. One, two, four, eight.
Five is four plus one, so it's one, zero, one. A byte is eight bits, so it holds zero to two fifty-five.
Instead of sending pieces, we'll send mixes of pieces. The mixing move is called ex-or.
Line two numbers up in bits. Wherever the second has a one, flip that bit of the first, like a light switch.
Five is one, zero, one. Seven is one, one, one. What's five ex-or seven?
Zero, one, zero. Two. And flip twice, and you're back where you started. Two ex-or seven is five again.
Each packet says which pieces it mixed, and the result. That's an equation. We'll draw each packet as a card.
The same cards as a grid. A row per card, and a dot where it uses a piece.
Solving works like in algebra class. Ex-or card one with card three, and A cancels. B ex-or C is four.
Put that into card two, and D is two. And so on.
The phone is just a bucket. It doesn't care which cards arrive, or in what order. It needs enough useful ones. Useful means it tells you something you couldn't already work out.
Here's a fifth card. B ex-or C is four. Is it useful?
No. You could make it yourself from cards one and three.

A sender can make endless fresh mixes, like water from a fountain, so these are called fountain codes. Both sides own the same shuffled deck, so a packet's number tells the phone which pieces it mixed.
The fountain code we'll open up is called RaptorQ, an internet standard since twenty eleven. This video is about the arithmetic inside it.
Use three pieces for a moment. A card either uses a piece or it doesn't, so there are eight possible cards, from nothing at all to A, B and C together.
Put them on the corners of a cube. One direction per piece. Step along A if the card uses A.
With one useful card, A, you can make two things, nothing or A. Add B, and you can make four. Each useful card doubles what you can make.
Two cards in hand. The next card is random. Each piece goes in or stays out by a coin flip. What's the chance it's useless?
Four lit corners out of eight. Half.
So for three random cards in a row, how often are all three useful?
Seven eighths, times six eighths, times four eighths. About one time in three, so it fails two times in three. With many pieces it fails seventy-one percent of the time. Call it the ex-or lottery.
Watch this danger meter as the bucket fills. For almost the whole fill, a random card is nearly certain to help. Almost all the danger is in the last few slots.
Three slots from the end, a random card is useless one time in eight. Then one in four. At the last slot, one in two. Ten pieces or ten million, the answer is about seventy-one percent.
Spares help. With two spare cards, how often does the lottery still fail?
Nearly one time in four. The first spare takes it from seventy-one to forty-two percent, and each one after that roughly halves it. With a million phones, that's almost a quarter of a million stuck.
Reaching one in a million takes about twenty spares. Ten halvings make about a thousand. Twenty make about a million.
And sometimes it's structure, not luck. Five cards in a ring, each the ex-or of two neighbours. Every letter appears twice, so together they cancel to nothing. The five are worth only four.

With only use it or don't, a card at the last slot is useless half the time, and the ring stays stuck. With two hundred fifty-six amounts, and the right arithmetic, it would almost never be. So what if a card could scale a piece? Three times A, or a hundred times A?
Then multiplying a byte must give a byte, and we must be able to undo it.
Bytes could wrap around at two fifty-six, like a clock. Mathematicians call that mod. But to undo times three, we must be able to divide.
Try two times one twenty-eight on this clock. What do you get?
The top bit slides off the end, and it's gone. Zero.
So a card saying two times A is six can't tell you A. It could be three, or one thirty-one.
Even amounts lose information, like two did. Odd ones never do. So with random byte amounts, only the last bit matters.
That's ex-or's coin flip again. This lottery fails seventy-one percent of the time, just like ex-or.
A prime number of hours fixes it. On a seven-hour clock, three times what is one?
Five. Every row of its times table, except zero's, is a reshuffle of all seven values. So every number but zero has a partner that multiplies it back to one, and that lets you divide.
Zero sneaks in at two fifty-six because two fifty-six is two times one twenty-eight. The nearest prime is two fifty-seven, but that clock needs an hour two fifty-six, which doesn't fit in a byte.

A number system where you can add, subtract, multiply, and divide by anything but zero, with all the usual rules of algebra, is called a field. We need one with exactly two hundred fifty-six members. So catch the falling bit, and fold it back in.
We need something like a prime, with two hundred fifty-six members. Whole numbers can't do it, but polynomials can.
Remember the place values, one, two, four, eight? Swap the two for an x. One, x, x squared, x cubed. Three was two plus one, so now it's x plus one.
The numbers in front are only zero or one, and one plus one is zero, like flipping a switch twice. So x plus x is zero, and adding is ex-or again.
Three is x plus one, and seven is x squared plus x plus one. Multiply them out, remembering that one plus one is zero. What do you get?
Six terms, and two pairs match. x squared plus x squared vanishes, and so does x plus x. What's left is x cubed plus one, which is one, zero, zero, one. Nine.
Three times seven is nine.
A product past x to the seventh doesn't fit in a byte. The simplest fold drops the fallen bit back in at the bottom. A rotation.
But under that fold, what is three times two fifty-five?

Zero. The rotation secretly treats x to the eighth plus one as zero, and x to the eighth plus one splits into x plus one, times a long polynomial. That's three times two fifty-five. Two fifty-six was two times one twenty-eight all over again.
So we need a polynomial that can't split. A prime polynomial. RaptorQ's rule is that whenever an x to the eighth falls off, you swap in x to the fourth plus x cubed plus x squared plus one.
Two times one twenty-eight is x to the eighth. Fold it, and you get sixteen plus eight plus four plus one. Twenty-nine. Not zero.
And every nonzero byte now has a partner. Two times one forty-two is exactly one.
A famous encryption standard picked a different prime polynomial. Then the same two bytes can multiply to different answers, so both ends must agree.
Start at one and keep multiplying by two. One, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, one twenty-eight. What comes next?
Twenty-nine. Keep going, and you visit every nonzero byte exactly once before coming back. Two hundred fifty-five steps.
Now move every nonzero byte to the step where it was reached. The star untangles into a circle.
Times two is one click around. A clock with two hundred fifty-five hours. Call it the byte clock.
To multiply, add clicks, just as two cubed times two to the fourth is two to the seventh. One twenty-eight times four. Seven clicks plus two is nine clicks. Fifty-eight.
One fifty times three? One fifty is a hundred eighty clicks, and three is twenty-five. Together, two hundred five clicks, which is one sixty-seven. That click count is called a logarithm.
That's how the standard multiplies. Look up two click counts, add them, and look up the answer. And every byte's partner sits at its mirror image across the top.
The wrong clock had two hundred fifty-six hours, and multiplying on it broke. The right one has two hundred fifty-five, and going around it is multiplying.
Every pair at once. Here's the whole times table in byte order. It looks like noise.

Sorted by clicks, it's perfect diagonal stripes. Each stripe is one total of clicks.
Now give every card random byte amounts. This design really exists. RaptorQ does something cheaper, but first see why it's so good.
Remember the last slot. Half the corners were lit, so a random ex-or card was useless half the time.
With random byte amounts, how often is a card useless at the last slot?
Only one time in two fifty-six. Scaling by a nonzero byte reshuffles all two fifty-six values, so exactly one choice of amount lands in the lit part.
So every extra card divides the risk by two fifty-six. With ex-or, each extra card only roughly halves it.
Let's race them on ten pieces. Keep adding random cards until every piece is pinned down, a thousand times over. Ex-or needs one or two spares on average. Byte cards almost never need even one.
One subtlety. A bigger field gains nothing if the amounts are still only zeros and ones. All the gain comes from the other two fifty-four values.

So use random byte amounts everywhere? Solving cards that each use every piece takes about the number of pieces, cubed, over three. For fifty thousand pieces, that's about forty-two trillion steps. At a billion a second, half a day.
Fast codes keep cards sparse. Each card mixes only a few pieces. About half mix two, and a few mix many.
Then decoding is a chain reaction, like Sudoku. A card with one unknown left gives it away. Remove that piece everywhere, and new single-unknown cards appear. This is called peeling.
Lose the card that starts it. What happens?
Nothing moves.

With exactly enough sparse cards, peeling usually gets stuck early. Even with two percent extra, most runs stall around ninety-eight percent. That sounds great, but over a hundred pieces are missing, and the picture is broken.
About one piece in a hundred and twenty isn't in any card. No decoder can find it.

Reed-Solomon codes are ideal. Any set of exactly enough packets rebuilds the picture. But the sender must decide in advance how many packets exist, and with byte arithmetic that tops out around two hundred fifty-six. A fountain never runs dry.
RaptorQ does something cheaper. Its packets never use byte amounts. Every one is a plain ex-or card.

Before sending, both sides agree on extra cards that tie the pieces together by fixed rules. They're never sent, so the phone gets them free. Only ten to sixteen of them are byte cards, whatever the block size. In big blocks, hundreds of others are cheap ex-ors.

Remember the danger meter. The ex-or cards fill the bucket to just short of full, before the danger starts. The byte cards fill the last ten to sixteen slots, where a card is useless only one time in two fifty-six.
What if those last cards were ex-or too?
The ex-or lottery again. About seventy-one percent failure. With the byte cards, about six in a thousand.
Back to the stuck Sudoku. In big blocks, RaptorQ's decoder mostly peels. When it's stuck, it parks one stubborn piece. We don't know C, so call it little c, and carry it along like x in algebra.
A is two ex-or c. B is six ex-or two ex-or c. D is six ex-or six ex-or two, so c cancels. And E follows from D.

At the end, the leftover cards and the byte cards pin down the parked pieces. Here c is fifteen ex-or fourteen ex-or six, which is seven. It's elimination in a clever order, so it works exactly when the cards pin down every piece.
Now the ring of five that ex-or couldn't solve. Let one byte card join it, E plus two times A is six. Walk around the ring. What do you get?

With ex-or, A met itself and cancelled. Now A plus two A is three A, because adding amounts is ex-or too, and one ex-or two is three. Three A is fifteen, so A is five. The same A, B, C, and D as at the start.
We ran a real RaptorQ decoder a million times, on small blocks of ten pieces. With exactly enough packets, it failed six thousand three hundred sixteen times. About six in a thousand.
Each extra card divides the risk by about two fifty-six. So with one extra packet, how many failures?
Twenty-four. Two extra, just once. That's too rare to measure precisely, and the rare unlucky phone just waits for one more packet.
The standard promises at most one in a hundred, one in ten thousand, and one in a million, averaged over random packets, for every block size it supports.
The originals can go first, unchanged, so a phone with a clean connection does no decoding at all.

It's in the standard for next-generation TV broadcasts. Its older sibling was chosen for mobile broadcast in two thousand five. And the same byte field protects disk arrays that survive two dead drives, and every QR code.
Two extra packets buy the standard's one in a million, because every nonzero byte has a partner to divide by. And that's because a polynomial refuses to factor. Three times seven is nine.
